Secretary advised Bachowski by letter that “[bjased on the investigative 
findings, it has been determined * * * that civil action to set aside the 
challenged election is not warranted.”
Bachowski sought judicial review under the APA. On appeal, the Third 
Circuit rejected the Secretary’s claim that the LMRDA precluded review, 
finding the principle of “absolute prosecutorial discretion” inapphcable, and 
clarifying that it “should be limited to those civil cases which, like criminal 
prosecutions, involve the vindication of societal or governmental interests, 
rather than the protection of individual rights.” 502 F.2d 79 (3d Cir. 1974). 
Rather, the court determined that the LMRDA was intended to vindicate the 
rights of “individual union members” who, without secretarial intervention, 
“are left without a remedy.” The circuit court also thought section 482(b) 
provided law to apply to review of the Secretary’s enforcement discretion. The 
court read that section as mandating prosecution if an investigation yielded 
probable cause to beheve that a violation had occurred affecting the outcome 
of an election, and no settlement remedying the violation could be reached. 
Without elaboration, the Supreme Court agreed in a footnote with the Third 
Circuit’s determination that the Secretary’s decision was not “an unreviewable 
exercise of prosecutorial discretion,” Hkewise holding that review was 
available. 421 U.S. at 568 n.7.
The Supreme Court ultimately held that the Secretary was obfiged to 
provide a list of reasons supporting his determination in order to fadhtate 
review by a court. Justice Rehnquist objected vigorously to the Court’s holding, 
arguing that it fell far outside the scope of the question on which certiorari was 
granted, namely “[w]hether a disappointed union office seeker may invoke the 
judicial process to compel the Secretary of Labor to bring an action under Title 
IV of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959 to set aside 
a union election.” Interestingly, although the Court held that courts were 
entitled to review the Secretary’s reasoning for his decision, it also cautioned 
that review should be extremely fight:
The necessity that the reviewing court refrain from substitution 
of its judgment for that of the Secretary thus helps define the 
permissible scope of review. Except in what must be the rare case, 
the court’s review should be confined to examination of the “reasons” 
statement, and the determination whether the statement, without 
more, evinces that the Secretary’s decision is so irrational as to
